lectureMeta: Workbook Q11-Q13, Q16-Q21, Q63. Tests [[04 - Contraception]].
stem: Which of the following is not a feature of combined oral contraceptives?
answer: The correct answer is D. Combined OCPs do not impact bone mineral density — that is a feature of progestin-only contraceptives (notably Depo-Provera).

weekLabel: Week 4 - Gynecology: Contraception, STIs, Pelvic Pain & Menopause
lectureMeta: Workbook Q11-Q13, Q16-Q21, Q63. Tests [[04 - Contraception]].
stem: A 36-year-old woman with a 10-year smoking history comes into your clinic for advice regarding contraceptives. She would like to have a transdermal patch. Which of the following is true for this woman?

options.html: There are no contraindications; she can begin the transdermal patch.
There are contraindications; recommend combined OCP
There are contraindications; recommend Depo-Provera injections
No hormone-containing methods of birth control would be safe for her to use; recommend copper IUD or condom use.

answer: The correct answer is C. Smoking is an absolute contraindication to estrogen-containing contraception in women over 35 — which rules out the OCP, the patch and the NuvaRing. Depo-Provera (progesterone injection) may be used in those with contraindications to estrogen. The Mirena IUS would be another progesterone-only option, so D overstates the restriction.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q11-Q13, Q16-Q21, Q63. Tests [[04 - Contraception]].
stem: Which of the following contraceptive methods has the lowest rate of pregnancy, including cases of imperfect use?
answer:
The correct answer is B. Mirena (levonorgestrel IUS) offers the best protection from pregnancy — better even than male and female sterilization. Failure rates per 1000 women in the first year of use:

MethodUnintended pregnancies / 1000
Levonorgestrel IUS (Mirena)1
Female sterilization5
copper IUD8
Injectable (Depo-Provera)30

stem: Julie, a 20-year-old university student comes to see you in your practice. She has never used anything but condoms for her contraceptive needs and is looking for additional protection. From friends she has heard that spotting is a common side-effect of some contraception. She would like to try to avoid this as she feels it would interfere with her life. Which of the following options would you suggest to offer the most protection and meet her needs?
answer: The correct answer is B. Both the IUS and the POP carry a risk of irregular bleeding and spotting, especially at first — which is exactly what she wants to avoid. A diaphragm would not affect bleeding patterns but has a much higher pregnancy risk, especially with imperfect use. The NuvaRing is the best of the four: menstruation should occur regularly during the fourth week, when the device is removed. She will need reminding that the NuvaRing does not protect against STIs.

weekLabel: Week 4 - Gynecology: Contraception, STIs, Pelvic Pain & Menopause
lectureMeta: Workbook Q11-Q13, Q16-Q21, Q63. Tests [[04 - Contraception]].
stem: Which of the following contraception options would you prescribe for someone with a history of migraine with aura?
answer: The correct answer is B. migraine with aura raises the risk of blood clots, so estrogen-containing methods are contraindicated because they compound that risk. The only progesterone-only option listed is the Mirena. Note that although the estrogen in the NuvaRing acts mostly locally, some is absorbed systemically through the vaginal mucosa — so it is not a workaround.

weekLabel: Week 4 - Gynecology: Contraception, STIs, Pelvic Pain & Menopause
lectureMeta: Workbook Q11-Q13, Q16-Q21, Q63. Tests [[04 - Contraception]].
stem: Which of the following is an absolute contraindication to the combined oral contraceptive pill?
answer:
The correct answer is C. Undiagnosed vaginal bleeding is an absolute contraindication to the combined OCP — you must not mask a bleed you have not explained.

Several distractors are actually indications: COCP is used in women not desiring fertility with endometriosis, adenomyosis (A), PCOS, dysmenorrhea, irregular menstruation (E), and acne/hirsutism. One benefit of COCP is the reduction of ovarian cysts (B). And note the qualifier on D: uncontrolled hypertension is an absolute contraindication, controlled hypertension is not.

weekLabel: Week 4 - Gynecology: Contraception, STIs, Pelvic Pain & Menopause
lectureMeta: Workbook Q11-Q13, Q16-Q21, Q63. Tests [[04 - Contraception]].
stem: Which of the following methods of contraception cannot be initiated immediately post-partum or post-termination?
answer: The correct answer is E. The NuvaRing is the only listed method containing both estrogen and progesterone, which is what makes it inappropriate immediately post-partum or post-termination. Depo-Provera, the Copper T, the POP and the Mirena are all progesterone-only or non-hormonal, and all are options.

stem: A 28-year-old woman comes into your clinic with genital bleeding, of which no cause has been yet found. She is using a combination of condoms and Depo-Provera injections as methods of birth control. Which of the following is true?

options.html: She can continue with her methods of birth control.
She should stop Depo-Provera but continue with condom use.
She should stop Depo-Provera, continue with condom use, and switch to combined OCP.
She should stop Depo-Provera, continue with condom use, and switch to EVRA patches.
She should stop Depo-Provera, continue with condom use, and switch to IUD.

answer: The correct answer is B. Undiagnosed genital bleeding is an absolute contraindication to Depo-Provera, the combined OCP, EVRA patches and the IUD — which eliminates C, D and E as substitutes. It is not a contraindication to condom use.

stem: A young woman comes to the Emergency Department after having unprotected sex three days ago. She is worried about pregnancy and asks you for emergency contraception. You complete a history and physical exam. On exam the patient has normal vital signs, a non-tender abdomen and no signs of infection on speculum exam. She has no known medical conditions. Your first step in the management of this patient should be which of the following?

options.html: A prescription for a copper IUD
Instructions on how to obtain Plan B from her community pharmacy
A prescription for the Yuzpe method emergency contraceptives

answer:
The correct answer is C. The best emergency contraceptive here is the copper IUD — it has the lowest failure rate of the available methods:

MethodFailure rate
Copper IUD0.1%
Plan B11%
Yuzpe method25%

But a pregnancy test is required before placing a copper IUD, because of the risk to an already-implanted pregnancy. The question asks for the first step, so the test comes before the device.

stem: A 22-year-old woman had unprotected intercourse 6 days ago. She has a negative pregnancy test and wants emergency contraception. Which option is still effective?
answer: The correct answer is E. The copper IUD works up to 7 days after unprotected intercourse, is the most effective method, and leaves her with ongoing contraception. This year's lecture gives levonorgestrel and ulipristal up to 5 days, levonorgestrel being most effective within 72 hours. So on day 6 only the copper IUD is left.

stem: Which of the following is a contraindication to inserting an IUD?

options.html: PID treated with antibiotics 3 years ago

answer: The correct answer is A. The absolute list is short: pregnancy, current PID or cervicitis, immediately after a septic abortion, a distorted uterine cavity, unexplained bleeding, malignant trophoblastic disease, pelvic TB (and PR+ breast cancer for the hormonal IUD). Smoking, age, nulliparity, HIV and a past PID are distractors, not contraindications.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q69-Q75. Tests [[04 - Contraception]].
stem: You are interviewing Tara, a new patient who is 16 years old. She tells you her cycles are 28 days long, and she menstruates for 5 days. By mid cycle, it would be reasonable to expect:

options.html: Corpus luteum, baseline body temperature, surge in progesterone, endometrium growth
Ovulation, rise in body temperature, surge in luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone, endometrium growth
Ovulation, rise in body temperature, baseline luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone, endometrium growth
Corpus luteum, rise in body temperature, baseline luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone, endometrium growth
Corpus albicans, baseline body temperature, slow rise in luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone, endometrium shedding

answer:
The correct answer is B. Walk the cycle:

  • Follicular phase: FSH stimulates follicle growth, and the growing follicle releases more and more estrogen. At this stage estrogen acts on LH and FSH via negative feedback.
  • Midcycle: estrogen peaks and flips to positive feedback on LH and FSH. The LH surge stimulates ovulation.
  • Secretory/luteal phase: the remaining corpus luteum secretes progesterone, preparing the uterus for implantation.

So at midcycle you expect ovulation, a rise in body temperature, a surge in LH and FSH, and a growing endometrium.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q69-Q75. Tests [[04 - Contraception]].
stem: ET, a 21-year-old university student comes into your walk-in clinic and tells you that they want to start having sex with their partner and would like to begin taking birth control pills. Their cycles usually are about 25-28 days, with their period lasting 4-6 days. In taking a history from ET, which of the following would stop you from prescribing oral contraceptives for ET?

options.html: They experience regular headaches, and takes acetaminophen (Tylenol®) as needed
They smoke half a pack a day
Their mother was diagnosed with breast cancer 2 years ago and is currently undergoing treatment
They have noticed some spotting that started 3 weeks ago that hasn't stopped
Their previous family doctor diagnosed them with endometriosis, and prescribed them mefenamic acid (Ponstan®) as needed

answer:
The correct answer is D. Undiagnosed vaginal bleeding is an absolute contraindication to starting oral contraceptives.

Each distractor is a near-miss version of a real contraindication:

  • B — smoking would be absolute if ET were 35 or older; at 21 it is not.
  • C — a first-degree relative's history of breast cancer is not a contraindication; a personal history is.
  • E — OCPs are commonly used to treat endometriosis.

Absolute contraindications to the OCP:

  • Active thrombophlebitis
  • Smokers > 35
  • Obstructive liver disease
  • Migraines with focal signs
  • Personal history of breast cancer
  • Undiagnosed genital bleeding

stem: After your expert history and physical, you have decided to prescribe Alesse® (a combined oral contraceptive) for your patient. You make sure to tell them about birth control use including risks and adverse effects. In which of the following situations should they immediately stop using Alesse® and see a doctor?

options.html: Severe unilateral leg pain, swelling, or tenderness

answer:
The correct answer is A. Severe unilateral leg pain or tenderness could be thrombophlebitis — patients must stop the OCP and seek medical attention.

Note the distinction the question is drawing: in the other situations patients should seek medical attention but do not need to discontinue the OCP.

stem: Five months after their previous visit, ET tells you that they has noticed their acne worsened while taking Alesse®. They wonder if there was a different brand they could try that will help with the acne. When suggesting alternative brands to try, which of the following is most important to keep in mind?
answer: The correct answer is B. For worsening acne on the OCP, the factor that matters when switching brands is choosing one with less androgenic activity. Examples of low-androgen progestins: drospirenone and ethynodiol diacetate. This is the same principle behind Q13.

stem: Several years later, ET tells you that they have started medical school and are currently running 7 clubs. They find that they are not able to take birth control pills regularly. They have in fact stopped taking them for the past 7 months and have been using condoms. They would like you to recommend another form of hormonal contraceptive, since they liked how OCPs shortened their periods and reduced pain from cramps. Which of the following would you NOT suggest?

options.html: High dose levonorgestrel (Plan B®) after intercourse

answer: The correct answer is C. Plan B® can be used as a form of birth control only if the couple has intercourse occasionally (e.g. a couple of times a year). It is not suitable for ET, who has regular intercourse and is also seeking the non-contraceptive benefits (shorter, less painful periods) that ongoing hormonal contraception provides.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q129-Q130. Tests [[05 - Abortion]], [[09 - Dilation and Curettage]].
stem: A 34-year-old patient undergoes a D&C while she was 8 weeks pregnant. 48 hours after the procedure, she presents to the ED with pain in her abdomen. Vitals: HR 120, BP 100/80, T 39ºC, SpO2 98% on room air. On P/E, guarding and rebound tenderness is noted. What complication of a D&C might have occurred here?
answer:
The correct answer is B. Complications of a D&C: cervical shock, uterine perforation, hemorrhage, hematometra (blood accumulating in the uterus).

The stem describes peritonitis — signs of infection, rebound tenderness, guarding — which points to uterine perforation. A is excluded on timing: cervical shock is a vasovagal reaction to paracervical block that lasts only a few minutes, not 48 hours.

stem: Ms. Jones a 25 year old woman presents to your office. She is complaining of a curd like discharge, vaginal discharge and pruritus. She also mentions that lately it hurts when she has sex with her boyfriend. She asks if you know what is wrong with her and if there is anything you can do. Based on the information given, what is your diagnosis?

options.html: Vaginitis caused by a foreign body

answer:
The correct answer is C. Candida causes the characteristic curd-like discharge. Contrast the discharges:

  • Candida → thick, curd-like; plus pruritus, vaginal dryness, dyspareunia. Onset often coincides with menses and intercourse.
  • Trichomonas → profuse, watery, frothy
  • Bacterial vaginosis → thin, white/grey

stem: A 26-year-old female presents to your clinic for complaints of foul and “fishy” smelling vaginal discharge that is grey in colour. Her medications only consist of a Mirena IUD. You perform some investigations and here are the results: Wet mount reveals 22% clue cells, pH of discharge is 5.7, and a positive Whiff test. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

She meets the Amsel criteria, and the Amsel criteria are how bacterial vaginosis is diagnosed. Any three of four make the diagnosis, and she has three: pH above 4.5 (hers is 5.7), more than 20% clue cells (22%), and a positive amine or “whiff” test. The fourth, a homogeneous grey-white discharge thinly coating the walls, is what she describes.

The whiff test is what excludes the other two infections. The lecture records it as negative in both trichomoniasis and candidiasis, so a positive whiff points away from A and D before you reach anything else.

And the discharge does not fit them either. Trichomonas (A) is profuse, purulent and yellow-green, classically with a strawberry cervix. Candidiasis (D) is thick, white and cottage-cheese-like, adherent to the walls, and itches. Atrophic vaginitis (C) needs a hypoestrogenic state, which a 26-year-old does not have.

The Mirena is not incidental. An intrauterine device is on the lecture's risk-factor list for BV, alongside a new partner, douching and smoking.

stem: Which of the following statements is not a difference between bacterial vaginosis (BV) and candidiasis?

options.html: Candidiasis is caused by a fungal agent while BV is caused by a bacterial agent
Candidiasis is treated using metronidazole while BV is treated using Miconazole or Fluconazole
Candidiasis will show budding yeast, hyphae or pseudohyphae on wet mount while BV will show increased clue cells on wet mount
Candidiasis will present with cottage cheese like discharge while BV will present with thin white/grey vaginal discharge

answer:
The correct answer is B. Read the options against the lecture's own comparison table and B is the one that fails.

C states that candidiasis shows budding yeast, hyphae or pseudohyphae on wet mount while BV shows clue cells. That is exactly what the lecture says, so it is a difference between them.

B has the two treatments the wrong way round. Metronidazole treats bacterial vaginosis; miconazole and fluconazole are the antifungals and treat candidiasis. As written, B is a false statement rather than a real difference, which makes it the option that does not describe how the two conditions differ.

A and D are both genuine differences and are stated correctly: the causative agents (fungal versus a shift to anaerobe-predominant flora — Gardnerella, Mobiluncus, Mycoplasma), and the discharge (thick cottage cheese versus thin grey-white).

answer: The correct answer is A. Trichomoniasis is an STI: oral metronidazole only (single dose or a week), and treat partners from the last 6 months or it simply returns. stem: A 27-year-old woman with a new sexual partner reports a fishy vaginal odour, worse after intercourse, with little itch. There is a thin grey discharge coating the vaginal walls, pH 5.0, and clue cells on wet mount. Which statement about her diagnosis is correct?

options.html: It is an STI and partners must be treated
It is not an STI but raises STI risk
Culture is required to confirm it
It is treated only in pregnancy

answer: The correct answer is B. This is bacterial vaginosis (Amsel: pH over 4.5, clue cells, fishy amine odour, thin homogeneous discharge). BV is the #1 infectious vaginitis and is not an STI, but it potentiates acquiring one, which is half the reason to treat it. Culture is not required; treatment is metronidazole (oral or vaginal), and in pregnancy it must be oral.

Thick discharge sticking to the vaginal wall

stem: Sarah, a 19-year-old woman comes to your clinic complaining of painful urination, increased urinary frequency and purulent discharge. A swab of the discharge reveals Neisseria gonorrhea. You call Sarah back in to let her know and to start her on treatment. What is your treatment plan?
answer: The correct answer is A. Treatment for gonorrhea is ceftriaxone 250 mg IM or cefixime 400 mg PO, plus azithromycin 1 g PO to cover possible co-infection with chlamydia. The dual-therapy principle is the point — you always cover chlamydia alongside gonorrhea.

stem: Which of the following is correct?

options.html: the primary stage of syphilis has a rash on the palms and feet
the treatment of syphilis is penicillin
the tertiary stage of syphilis has the formation of a painless ulcer
the secondary stage of syphilis can last 20 years
the latent stage of syphilis can affect the heart eyes and brain

answer:
The correct answer is B. The treatment of syphilis is penicillin. The other options scramble the staging:

  • Primary — formation of a painless ulcer (chancre); highly contagious
  • Secondary — lasts 4-6 weeks; rash on the palms and feet, headaches, fever
  • Latent — can last 20 years; asymptomatic carriers
  • Tertiary — systemic; may affect the heart, eyes and brain

stem: Janet is a 32-year-old woman who presents to your office complaining of malaise, headache and genital sores. You take her vitals and notice that she has a fever. Upon examination you note blisters on the mucosal surface of the genital area, some of which have formed shallow ulcers and are very painful. Based on the most likely diagnosis what is your treatment plan?
answer: The correct answer is C. The presentation — especially blisters that break down into shallow, very painful ulcers — is genital herpes (HSV-2). Since this is viral, antibiotics are the wrong class entirely; acyclovir is an antiviral and is the right choice.

stem: Which of the following regarding HPV is true:

options.html: HPV 6 can produce LSILs, HSILs, and warts

answer: The correct answer is D. HPV 6 and 11 are the non-oncogenic (wart) types; HPV 6 does not produce HSILs, so A is false. HPV 16 and 18 are oncogenic, produce both HSILs and LSILs, and are responsible for >70% of all cervical cancer cases — so B and C are both false.

stem: A 43yr old women with irregular menstrual cycles presents for postcoital vaginal bleeding. As part of your work up, you order a pap smear. The results from the smear read – high grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL). What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
answer:
The correct answer is A. HSIL is an immediate referral to colposcopy.

HSIL is a high-grade result, and the high-grade branch of the algorithm has only one exit: colposcopy, immediately. The screening lecture splits abnormal cytology in two. The low-grade group — LSIL and ASC-US — is repeated in 6 to 12 months, because most low-grade change resolves on its own. The high-grade group — HSIL, ASC-H and squamous cell carcinoma — is referred for colposcopy without an intervening test.

C and D are the low-grade arm applied to a high-grade result. Waiting 12 months (C) is the LSIL rule, and repeating the cytology immediately (D) tests the same cells with the same test and cannot downgrade what has already been reported.

B inverts the order of the algorithm. HPV DNA testing sits upstream of cytology in primary HPV screening: a positive HPV sample goes on to cytology, and a positive cytology goes on to colposcopy. Once you are holding an HSIL you are already past the point HPV testing informs, and her postcoital bleeding at 43 makes delay the wrong direction to move in.

Repeat the Pap smear in 3 years according to the standard protocol
Send the patient for an HPV DNA test

answer:
The correct answer is C. The result cannot exclude high-grade changes, so she needs more thorough investigation and treatment at a colposcopy clinic.

A (repeat in 6 months) would be correct if the result had been LSIL or ASCUS. D is wrong because the HPV DNA test is not used in women under 30.

stem: Which of the following is not a long-term complication of pelvic inflammatory disease?
answer:
The correct answer is C. A pelvic abscess is a sign of active infection, so it is a short-term sequela of PID, not a long-term complication.

The genuine long-term complications: ectopic pregnancy (tubes blocked by adhesions), chronic pelvic pain, infertility (same mechanism as the ectopic), and PID may also make hysterectomy and BSO necessary.

stem:
Which of the following infections are diagnosed using serology?

  1. Chlamydia
  2. Gonorrhea
  3. Syphilis
  4. Hepatitis B
  5. HIV
answer:
The correct answer is D.

From 08 - Approach to Sexually Transmitted Infections. Split the list by what can be sampled directly. Syphilis will not grow in culture, so it is diagnosed by darkfield microscopy and serology (VDRL screen, fluorescent treponemal antibody to confirm). Hepatitis B is read off a serology panel (HBsAg, IgM anti-HBc, anti-HBs). HIV is diagnosed by the HIV 1/2 Ag/Ab combination immunoassay. That is iii, iv, v.

  • A, B, C each include chlamydia and/or gonorrhea, which are diagnosed by direct sampling of the organism - cervical/vaginal swab or first-catch urine > 2 h since voiding (NAAT) - not by antibodies.

Principle: bloodborne/systemic infections are serology; mucosal bacterial STIs are swab or urine.

stem: Which of the following symptoms is present during the secondary stage of syphilis infection?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Condyloma lata is the lesion of secondary syphilis — large, flat warts, which the lecture is careful to distinguish from the cauliflower-like condylomata acuminata of HPV. It appears alongside the rest of the secondary picture: systemic symptoms, and the characteristic non-itchy rash on the palms and soles.

The other three are the other stages. The painless chancre (A) is primary. Gummatous disease (C) is tertiary. The CNS complications in D — meningitis, stroke, seizures — are neurosyphilis, which the lecture groups with late disease rather than with the secondary stage.

The stage split is the whole point of the question: syphilis is staged by what it is doing to the skin and nervous system at the time, and the treatment (penicillin G) is the same while the stage governs the dose and duration.

stem: A 50 y/o female patient presents with pelvic pain. Which of the following would NOT be consistent with a diagnosis of adenomyosis:

options.html: Patient has tender, symmetrically enlarged, "boggy" uterus
Uterine biopsy identifies no significant abnormalities.

answer:
The correct answer is A. Adenomyosis is proliferation of endometrial tissue (stroma and/or glands) within the myometrium, with smooth muscle hypertrophy leading to uterine enlargement. The ectopic tissue traps blood, which irritates the myometrium.

It is uncommon in nulligravids, because it is the contraction of the uterus post-delivery that commonly drives the endometrial entrapment. The rest all fit: a tender, enlarged, "boggy" uterus (B); often asymptomatic but can associate with pelvic pain and abnormal bleeding (C); usually presents in the pre- or peri-menopausal period (D); and imaging may help but biopsy does not penetrate deep enough to be diagnostic (E).

stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the most common sites for endometriosis?
answer:
The correct answer is E. Endometriosis is endometrial tissue outside the uterus. It can occur anywhere via implantation, metaplasia or vascular/lymphatic spread — including the bladder — but the most common sites are the ovaries (chocolate cysts), uterine ligaments, pelvic peritoneum and rectovaginal septum.

Location drives presentation: endometriosis in the pouch of Douglas causes deep dyspareunia.

The correct answer is D. Diagnosis of endometriosis requires 2 of 3 on biopsy taken outside the uterus:

  3. hemosiderin

stem: Which of the following is the most common benign neoplasm in females?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Leiomyomas are the most common neoplasm in females — clinically apparent in about 25% of reproductive-age women — and the most common cause of abnormal uterine bleeding. They are benign smooth-muscle tumours, and the lecture is emphatic that they are not pre-malignant and not a precursor to malignancy.

The distractors are each a different kind of thing, which is what the question is really testing. An endometrial polyp (A) is a focal overgrowth and is common, but not on leiomyoma's scale. Adenomyosis (B) is endometrial glands within the myometrium — a process, not a neoplasm. Endometrial hyperplasia (D) is proliferation that is on the pathway to carcinoma, which makes it the conceptual opposite of a fibroid rather than a competitor for the same title.

stem: A 21-year-old sexually active female presents with bilateral lower abdominal pain radiating to the back. She has heavy vaginal bleeding, deep dyspareunia and vaginal discharge. Which of the following would help to rule out pelvic inflammatory disease?
answer:
The correct answer is E. Signs of PID include fever, adnexal tenderness, cervicitis, cervical motion tenderness and a pelvic mass. Investigations (CBC, electrolytes, βhCG, cultures) may show leukocytosis and positive cultures — and a positive βhCG should make you think ectopic pregnancy. U/S may show a pelvic mass or tubo-ovarian abscess.

The trick is the question's direction: A-D may or may not be present in PID, so none of them can rule it out — hence E. Laparoscopy may be done if the diagnosis is unsure, but if the clinical picture suggests PID, treat for PID — this is a diagnosis you do not want to miss.

stem: A 25 year old woman presents to the ED with severe pelvic pain which lateralizes to her right side. She is tachycardic and hypotensive but not feverish, and is experiencing vaginal bleeding as well. Her last menstrual period was 8 weeks ago. She realizes that she's been feeling nauseous and has had breast tenderness for the past 3 weeks. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is C. Features of ectopic pregnancy: lateralized pelvic pain, vaginal bleeding, pregnancy symptoms, and amenorrhea 6-12 weeks after LMP — she is at 8 weeks. If ruptured, add rectal pressure, tenesmus, shoulder tip pain and syncope; she is already tachycardic and hypotensive.

A — the acuity and pregnancy symptoms do not fit. B — would present with more urinary symptoms and probably fever. D — placenta previa is a cause of second trimester bleeding. E — spontaneous abortion does not often present with lateralizing pain.

stem: What initial investigations should be started for a man with fertility issues? Choose all that apply:
answer:
The correct answers are A, C and D. LH/FSH, semen analysis and testosterone form the initial work-up.

The other two are second-line, and conditional on those results:

  • Karyotype (B) — done based on the results of FSH, LH and testosterone (specifically low testosterone with high LH and FSH).
  • Testicular biopsy (E) — appropriate for azoospermic men with palpable vasa deferentia and normal FSH.

stem: Which of the following does not aid in successful transport of sperm in the female reproductive tract?

options.html: Large numbers of sperm per ejaculation

answer:
The correct answer is E. The fimbria of the fallopian tube move to help "pick up" the oocyte after its release from the ovary, but they do not play a role in sperm transport.

The others all do: low-viscosity mucus (A) lets sperm through the cervix, whereas thickened cervical mucus acts as a form of contraception; uterine contractions (B) move sperm by peristalsis-like action; the flagellum (C) propels the sperm; and sheer numbers (D) raise the probability that one succeeds, since only ~50-100 of an ejaculate actually reach the egg.

stem: You are consulted to see a couple trying for a baby for that past year. After a thorough work-up, you find that the female partner is anovulatory. Which of the following tests will NOT help to diagnose this?
answer:
The correct answer is D. A hysterosalpingogram assesses tubal patency — a mechanical question, not an ovulatory one.

All the others speak to ovulation: progesterone challenge test and FSH/LH report on the HPG axis; pelvic U/S shows masses or cysts on the ovaries; TSH/PRL detect ovulatory inhibitors. See infertility.

stem: Where does capacitation occur?
answer: The correct answer is A. Capacitation is the cellular and molecular changes that ejaculated spermatozoa must undergo in order to fertilize. It occurs while the sperm are in the fallopian tube. It is characterized by three accomplishments: 1) The ability to bind to the zona pellucida (noncellular porous layer of glycoproteins secreted by the oocyte; separates the oocyte from cumulus cells). 2) The ability to undergo acrosomal reaction. 3) The acquisition of hypermotility.

answer:
The correct answer is D. Indications for an endometrial biopsy are: abnormal uterine bleeding in all women over 40, or women under 40 who are at high risk of neoplasia or who have failed therapies for dysfunctional uterine bleeding. Neither applies to this patient.

Prolactin, LH and FSH, T4 and TSH, and hemoglobin are all appropriate for investigating her secondary amenorrhea; βhCG (already done) and androgens would be appropriate too.

answer:
The correct answer is D. All of these can stop abnormal uterine bleeding, but the question asks for the definitive treatment — and the only way to definitively treat her is to remove the uterus.

stem: Endometriosis can be treated with the following, except:
answer:
The correct answer is E.

From 10 - Endometriosis. Tubal occlusion appears in the lecture under complications, not treatment: endometriosis causes infertility partly via tubal occlusion (and impaired tubal transport from an inflamed pelvis). Occluding the tubes does nothing to estrogen-driven ectopic endometrium or its pain.

  • A NSAIDs - the mainstay is ovulatory suppression plus NSAID pain control.
  • B danazol - a testosterone derivative giving pseudomenopause (withdraws estrogen), alongside GnRH agonists.

stem: Which of the following would be classified as primary amenorrhea?

options.html: 16 y/o female has not had a period in 4 months.
18 y/o female athlete has not had a period in 12 months.
12 y/o female has never had a period.
18 y/o female has never had a period
18 y/o female with obesity, hirsutism, and severe acne has irregular periods, and has not had one in 4 months.

answer:
The correct answer is D. primary amenorrhea is generally defined as absence of periods by age 16; secondary amenorrhea is absence of 3 or more consecutive periods at some point after the first period. Girls with secondary amenorrhea generally have secondary sexual characteristics.

Working through the distractors: A (possibly pregnant), B (possibly exercise-related), E (possibly PCOS-related) are all secondary amenorrhea; C is not old enough to be considered to have amenorrhea at all. D still requires you to rule out pregnancy, but is primary amenorrhea because she has never had a period.

stem: You are working up a patient for primary amenorrhea. You have determined that she has delayed puberty. What is your next step?

options.html: Do a pelvic exam and/or ultrasound

answer:
The correct answer is B. After establishing that puberty is delayed, the first step is serum FSH and LH, because it localizes the lesion:

  • High FSH/LH → the problem is gonadal
  • Low FSH/LH → the problem is central (constitutional delay, anorexia, illness)

C (genetic analysis) becomes appropriate if FSH and LH come back high. A (pelvic exam/ultrasound) would be appropriate if puberty were normal. D and E point to secondary causes and so belong in the work-up of secondary amenorrhea, not this one.

stem: Which of the following is not a risk factor for contracting an STI?

options.html: Sexually active youth under 25 years of age.
No contraception or sole use of non-barrier methods of
All of the above are risk factors for STIs

answer:
The correct answer is E.

Every option listed is a recognised risk factor, which is why E is the answer. The public health lecture groups them rather than listing them flat, and all three named here fall inside the grouping:

  • Age — sexually active youth under 25, who carry a disproportionate share of chlamydia and gonorrhea (B).
  • Behaviour and exposure — injection drug use (A), which is why the lecture treats STIs and bloodborne infections together as STBBIs: the risk factors are shared.
  • Barrier use — no contraception, or a non-barrier method only (C). A non-barrier method prevents pregnancy and does nothing about transmission, and that gap is the point.
  • A previous STI (D), which marks both an exposure pattern and a partner network that has not changed.

A question whose options are all correct is testing whether you will talk yourself out of one. The useful move is to check each against the list rather than hunt for the odd one out.

stem: Which of the following are not a characteristic of Progestin?

options.html: Many POCs increase aldosterone production, leading to fluid retention and weight gain.
POCs thicken cervical mucus, making it difficult for sperm penetration
The effect of Progesterone on GnRH suppression is weaker than Estrogen’s effect
When taking POC, patient compliance is not as important

answer: The correct answer is D. It is paramount that POCs are taken at the same time, every single day, because progesterone’s effect on GnRH suppression is “weaker” as it only decreases the chance of ovulation suppression. It heavily relies on its secondary effects (i.e.,thickening of cervical mucus, alteration of tubal peristalsis, suppression of uterine contractility), and therefore these effects wane over time, reverting the endometrium back to the “receptive” condition.

stem: A 75 year old woman is being followed for an invasive carcinoma of the breast. It is estrogen receptor positive and Her2/neu negative. The patient has previously been diagnosed with osteoporosis. What medical treatment is the best choice?
answer: The workbook's answer is D. Its reasoning: raloxifene is a SERM — full antagonist in breast and endometrium, but partial agonist in bone, so estrogen's protective effects on bone continue, which suits a patient who also has osteoporosis.

flags.title: This answer is clinically wrong — verify before using it
flags.html: Raloxifene is not a treatment for established invasive breast cancer. It is licensed for osteoporosis and for risk reduction in high-risk women. For a 75-year-old with invasive ER+/HER2- disease, endocrine therapy is tamoxifen or an aromatase inhibitor — and tamoxifen is also a partial agonist in bone in postmenopausal women, so it delivers the very bone benefit the key credits only to raloxifene. On the actual clinical question, B is the better answer; the workbook appears to have swapped the two SERMs' indications.

stem: Which of the following are not offered methods of abortion in First Trimester?
answer:
The correct answer is E. This option is used in 2nd trimester abortion.

Intracardiac digoxin or KCl is a second-trimester step, not a first-trimester one. The lecture's table sets the feticidal injection before misoprostol induction in the second trimester, to 25 weeks. In the first trimester there is nothing for it to do.

The other four are all first-trimester methods:

  • Mifepristone + misoprostol (B), the medical route, to 70 days.
  • Methotrexate + misoprostol (C), the medical route used before mifepristone was approved in Canada in 2015 — less effective and slower, but offered, and to 49 days.
  • Manual vacuum aspiration (A), in the office, to 10 weeks.
  • Dilation and curettage (D), under 14 weeks.

The organising idea is that gestational age picks the method, and the feticidal agent only enters once the gestation is advanced enough to need one.

stem: Maria is a 24 y.o. woman with a history of depression who comes to you with a positive pregnancy test. Her depression has been well controlled on Fluoxetine, an SSRI antidepressant, for the past 6 years. She worries about the effect of this medication - what should you do?

options.html: Antidepressants are absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy, stop the drug immediately and refer to a psychologist for counseling in order to control her depression during her pregnancy
Fluoxetine is associated with malformations, therefore you should start her on a newer antidepressant which has not yet been shown to be associated with birth defects
In order to avoid withdrawal of both Maria and the fetus from the antidepressant, you should wean her off the drug slowly and remain drug-free for the duration of the pregnancy
Start another agent such as valproic acid in order achieve optimum control of her depression and prevent any deterioration during her pregnancy
Stay on the same dose of fluoxetine to maintain control of her depression

answer:
The correct answer is E. Depression in pregnancy is itself associated with bad outcomes, so maintaining treatment matters. Fluoxetine has been studied, and malformations arise at the same rate in fluoxetine-exposed women as in the general population.

B inverts the correct principle (see Q85D): it is better to use effective drugs with a long track record than newer alternatives that have not been studied as extensively. D is actively dangerous — valproic acid is known to cause neural tube defects and should not be added to a pregnant woman's regimen unless completely necessary.

stem: Tara's sister, Melissa, visits your office and tells you that even though she is 25 years old, she has never had a period. While conducting a history and physical, you start to formulate differential diagnoses for her complaint. Which of the following is not on your differential:
answer:
The correct answer is D. Amenorrhea can be caused by anorexia, hypothyroidism, Turner syndrome, pregnancy and imperforate hymen.

Hyperthyroidism may cause irregular periods (thyroid hormones act in a negative feedback loop on the hypothalamus) but not amenorrhea.

Note the deliberate trap in E: even though Melissa has never had a period, pregnancy still should not be ruled out as long as she is sexually active.

stem: Three months after seeing ET, they call you in a panic and tells you that they forgot to take her birth control pills for the past 2 days. They are currently in week 1 of the pill pack and had sex with their partner yesterday. What do you recommend?

options.html: Explain to them that since they had sex on one of the days they missed a pill, they are now pregnant. Refer them to the pregnancy options program.
Tell them to take two pills as soon as possible, then continue the rest of the pack as usual
Tell them to purchase and use emergency contraception (Plan B®) as soon as possible, and use another method of birth control for the next 7 days
Tell them since they have been taking their birth control pills regularly up to now, the medication has already reached steady state in their body, and they only need to resume their normal regimen.
Tell them to take Plan B® as soon as possible and use another method of birth control for the next 7 days. Resume the pack the day after.

answer:
The correct answer is E. The baseline rule for a missed pill is B — take two pills as soon as possible, then finish the pack as usual the next day (with the exception that if 2-4 pills were forgotten in the third week, discard the rest and start a new pack that day).

But this case triggers the escalation. Use Plan B® plus 7 days of backup, resuming the pack the day after, if the patient forgot a pill in the first week, OR forgot several pills during the cycle, OR forgot more than four in a row — AND has had intercourse in the five days prior. ET meets the first-week condition and the recent-intercourse condition.

Why the first week matters: the biggest risk of pregnancy occurs when the interval between two packs exceeds 7 days, or when a pill is missed in the first week, because the risk of ovulation is much higher.

She shares that she is not at the right place in life to have a baby, and would like to know her options for termination. You calculate that the products of conception are at 4 weeks gestational age. answer: The correct answer is E. At 4 weeks GA she is technically a candidate for all of these. stem: Which of the following groups of women should receive annual cervical cancer screening?

options.html: all women who are sexually active
women who have not received the Gardasil vaccine

answer:
The correct answer is A. Immunocompromised women should receive annual screening, because of their greater chance of developing an infection the immune system cannot clear.

Everyone else screens on the standard interval: women with multiple partners (B), sexually active women 21 or older (C), and — importantly — women who have had the Gardasil vaccine still require standard screening (D), because the vaccine only protects against a subset of HPV types. See cervical cancer.

stem: Which of the following is a cause of menometrorrhagia (bleeding too much and between periods)? Select all that apply.
answer:
The correct answers are A, B, E, F, H. Fibroids, anovulation, endometrial hyperplasia, endometrial malignancy and cervical malignancy all increase menstrual blood loss and cause bleeding between periods.

The distractors are all wrong-direction answers:

  • C Granulosa cell tumours secrete estrogen, and therefore decrease the frequency and volume of menstruation — as does G the COCP.
  • D Uterine synechiae cause hypomenorrhea.
  • I Ectropion affects neither frequency nor volume.

stem: Which of the following medications can result in abnormal uterine bleeding? Select all that apply.
answer:
The correct answer is G (all of the above).

  • Dopamine agonists affect prolactin secretion, which can in turn cause amenorrhea.

stem: Which one of the following is not part of the BRATS acronym for common genital injuries sustained from an acute sexual assault?
answer:
The correct answer is E. The S in BRATS is swelling, not soreness.

BRATS lists the observable genital injuries documented on examination: Bruises, Redness, Abrasions, Tears, Swelling. Each is a physical sign the examiner can see and record as medico-legal evidence.

  • A-D (bruises, redness, abrasions, tears) are all genuine letters of the mnemonic.
  • E fails because soreness is a symptom the survivor reports, not a sign the examiner documents - which is why the S is swelling.

stem: A 62-year-old woman presents with a three-week history of vaginal bleeding, associated with some cramping and pressure. She underwent menopause at the age of 52, and received hormone replacement therapy for her menopausal symptoms, which she has now stopped taking. Her pelvic exam is normal. Her biopsy reveals complex endometrial hyperplasia with atypia. What is the recommended treatment?
answer:
The correct answer is E. Complex endometrial hyperplasia with atypia carries a 29% risk of progression to malignancy, and first-line therapy is hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (also first line for simple hyperplasia with atypia).

  • High-dose progesterone (C) is for simple hyperplasia and complex hyperplasia without atypia, and is considered in atypia only where surgery is contraindicated.
  • Local estrogen (A) treats vaginal atrophy — the most common cause of post-menopausal bleeding, but not this.
  • B is a trap: hysterectomy by itself is not sufficient; the BSO is indicated as well.
  • HRT (D) is not indicated for endometrial hyperplasia.

stem: Post Menopausal Bleeding is any bleeding in post-menopausal woman after absense of menstrual flow for:
answer:
The correct answer is D.

The lecture's definition is exact: post-menopausal bleeding is any bleeding in a post-menopausal woman after the absence of menstrual flow for 12 months. It occurs in about 11% of post-menopausal women.

The threshold is doing real work rather than being a number to memorise. Twelve months is also what defines menopause itself, so the definition is saying that bleeding counts as post-menopausal once you are confident menopause has actually happened. Shorter intervals (A, C) fall inside perimenopause, where an irregular cycle is expected rather than alarming, and two years (B) would delay investigation of a symptom whose whole point is that it needs endometrial carcinoma excluded.

stem: Match the correct marker substance for each pathology.
answer:
The pairings:

PathologyMarker
DysgerminomaLDH
Yolk sac tumora-FP
Choriocarcinomab-hCG

Each germ cell tumour is named by the tissue it is trying to be, and the marker follows from that. The lecture's marker table sets out three strong associations:

  • Dysgerminoma → LDH. The ovarian counterpart of the seminoma; LDH is its marker.
  • Yolk sac tumour → alpha-fetoprotein. AFP is what a yolk sac makes, so a tumour differentiating towards yolk sac makes it too. Most common in toddlers, and Schiller-Duval bodies on histology are pathognomonic.
  • Choriocarcinoma → beta-hCG. It arises from placental tissue, and beta-hCG is the placental hormone.

Worth holding onto: immature teratoma and embryonal carcinoma each raise two of the three weakly, which is why the table marks the three above as the strong, discriminating associations rather than the only ones.

stem: Benefits of HRT include all of the following except?
answer:
The correct answer is D. HRT improves menopausal symptoms (and therefore quality of life), decreases osteoporosis risk and improves urogenital health.

stem: Which of the following occurs in menopause? Select all that applies.

options.html: Hot flashes, vaginal atrophy, vaginal dryness are common symptoms

answer:
The correct answer is A, D.

A and D both follow from the same event: the ovary stops responding. The remaining few oocytes become unresponsive to gonadotropins, so estrogen and progesterone production falls.

That falling estrogen is what causes A. Vasomotor symptoms — hot flashes, night sweats, perspiration, chills, palpitations — are the most prevalent symptoms, in 80–85% during menopause. Vaginal burning and dryness belong to the genitourinary group, alongside dyspareunia, dysuria, urgency and recurrent urinary tract infections.

And it is what causes D. With the ovary no longer producing estrogen, the negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary is lost, so LH and FSH rise. A raised FSH is the biochemical signature of menopause for exactly this reason.

B and C invert it. Estrogen and progesterone production falls rather than rises (C), and low estrogen means less vaginal hydration, not more (B) — that dryness is the same finding the question already gave you in A.

stem: Which of the following statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.html: Post menopausal women with history of hysterectomy can be on Estrogen-only HRT.
LET alleviates vasomotor symptoms, such as palpitations and perspirations
The 3 main causes of illness and disability in developed countries for postmenopausal women are: Stroke, decreased sexual drive, and cancer
During perimenopause, women often experience change in their cycle length & flow
As women transition from perimenopause to menopause, they experience oligomenorrhea and hypomenorrhea, until menstruation completely stops

answer:
The correct answer is A, D, E.

A is true because the progestin in HRT has one job: protecting the endometrium. Unopposed estrogen drives endometrial proliferation, so a woman with a uterus needs a progestin alongside it. After hysterectomy there is no endometrium to protect, so estrogen-only therapy is appropriate.

D and E are the perimenopausal transition as the lecture describes it. Cycle length and flow change first (D), and the pattern then moves through oligomenorrhea and hypomenorrhea until menstruation stops altogether (E).

B fails on the therapy, not the symptoms. Palpitations and perspiration are genuinely vasomotor symptoms, but local estrogen therapy is local: it treats the genitourinary symptoms — dryness, dyspareunia, urinary symptoms — and systemic therapy is what addresses vasomotor symptoms.

C misstates the list. The three main causes of illness and disability named for this group are cardiovascular disease, cancer, and osteoporosis-associated fractures. Reduced sexual drive is common — half of women report at least one sexual problem, most often reduced desire — but it is not one of the three, and stroke sits inside cardiovascular disease rather than beside it.

stem: What is the primary function of the spiral arteries in the uterus during pregnancy?

options.html: To supply oxygen and nutrients to the developing fetus
To provide a route for maternal blood to exit the uterus during delivery
To maintain the structural integrity of the uterus
To promote uterine contractions during labor

stem: Which of the following occurs as a physiological adaptation to pregnancy?
answer:
The correct answer is B. Red blood cell mass increases in pregnancy — but blood viscosity actually decreases, because the plasma volume increase outstrips the RBC increase (this is the physiologic anemia of pregnancy). So A is the wrong direction.

The rest of the adaptations, each the opposite of the option given:

  • To compensate for the lower viscosity, production of plasma clotting factors increases to limit blood loss at delivery — so E is backwards.
  • Blood flow increases to many organs including skin, uterus, kidneys and breasts — so D is backwards.
  • Oxygen consumption increases by ~20%, achieved via increased tidal volume and respiratory rate — so C is backwards.

stem: Which of the following is true of thyroid function in pregnancy?

options.html: Most women will experience clinically significant thyroid dysfunction at some point during their pregnancy
Thyroid binding globulin (TBG) levels decrease leading to freer T3 and T4 in circulation
Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) mimics TSH which leads to an increase in production of T4
Thyroid hormone supplementation is contraindicated in pregnancy as it can act as a teratogen
Circulating levels of T3 tend to be higher than T4 due to changes in protein metabolism and availability of thyroid binding globulin (TBG)

answer:
The correct answer is C. hCG mimics TSH, which drives more T4 production — but TBG levels also increase, so free T3 and T4 stay stable while total levels rise. That combination is why most pregnant women remain euthyroid despite the hormonal changes (A is false, B has TBG in the wrong direction).

D is emphatically false: thyroid supplementation is NOT contraindicated in pregnancy.

answer:

stem: A 28-year-old primigravida presents to the obstetrics clinic at 24 weeks gestation with complaints of headache and blurred vision. On examination, her blood pressure is 150/100 mmHg and her urine dipstick reveals 2+ proteinuria. Which of the following is a likely consequence of the abnormality of uterine spiral arteries seen in this patient?

options.html: Increased risk of fetal growth restriction
Increased risk of preterm premature rupture of membranes

answer:
The correct answer is C. This is pre-eclampsia — hypertension plus proteinuria developing after 20 weeks. One of the underlying mechanisms is thought to be abnormal remodeling of the uterine spiral arteries, which leads to inadequate blood flow to the placenta and therefore impaired fetal growth.

Fetal growth restriction is a common complication of pre-eclampsia and can cause significant morbidity and mortality if not managed, which is why close monitoring matters. Note that A and B are both the wrong direction — pre-eclampsia increases the risk of preterm labour and abruption.

stem: You see a patient who is concerned about a breast lump. On exam, the lump is fixed in its position, which may mean that the lump has invaded:
answer: The correct answer is D. A breast lump becoming fixed is highly suggestive of invasion into the retromammary space — the space between the pectoralis major muscle and the mammary tissue. Normally the breast moves freely over the chest wall because of the loose connective tissue in that space; tumour invasion adheres the lump to the chest wall, producing the "fixed" finding. None of the other options would explain fixation.

stem: Which of the following are NOT a potential complication of D&C?
answer:
The correct answer is E.

A, B, C and D are all on the lecture's complication list for the procedure itself: uterine perforation, hemorrhage (which may signal uterine atony, low implantation or a larger gestational age than expected), hematometra or post-abortal syndrome, and cervical shock. Infertility is not among them, which is what the key is pointing at.

Read it as “not an immediate complication” rather than “never a consequence”. The same lecture names curettage as a risk factor for intrauterine adhesions — about 8% after one procedure, rising towards 30% by a third within 24 hours — and trauma as the major cause of them. Adhesions are the mechanism behind Asherman syndrome, which does impair fertility.

So the distinction the question is really drawing is between what can go wrong during and just after a D&C and what can follow from repeated instrumentation over time.

stem: Which of the following procedure is recommended for patients with enlarged uterus?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

A large uterus is a contraindication to every minimally invasive route, so the abdominal approach is what is left. That is the pattern to take from this rather than the single answer: the lecture lists “large uterus” under contraindications for the vaginal approach (B), for laparoscopic-assisted vaginal hysterectomy (C), and for total or subtotal laparoscopic hysterectomy (D).

The routes are otherwise ranked the other way round. The lecture is explicit that if a patient's anatomy is amenable to a vaginal approach, that should be the first option, and the laparoscopic routes are framed as alternatives to an abdominal hysterectomy rather than as the default. Abdominal is the fallback when anatomy rules the others out, which is precisely the situation an enlarged uterus creates.

The vaginal route carries other contraindications worth holding alongside it: prior pelvic surgery, extensive scarring, a narrow introitus or pelvis, poor uterine descent, and a planned salpingectomy or salpingo-oophorectomy, since the tubes and ovaries are not readily reached through the vagina.

stem: A 40 y.o pregnant mom (in third trimester) presents with headache, blurry vision, fatigue, malaise, nausea/vomiting. She is found to have high liver enzymes, low plt, BP: 130/82. What is her most likely diagnosis, which should not be missed?
answer: The correct answer is A. The patient most likely has HELLP, which stands for hemolysis elevated liver enzymes low plt. Note that it is an typical form of pre-eclampsia/eclampsia so doesn’t require HTN for dx. Molar pregnancy (D) would likely present with extremely high hCG and painless vaginal bleeding. Theca lutein cyst (c) may present with pelvic heaviness, maternal virilization, and ruptured cysts may cause bleeding. Both molar pregnancy and theca lutein cyst would present in earlier pregnancy rather than third trimester and both are risk factors for pre-eclampsia. The patient doesn’t have clinical hypertension/pre-eclampsia though because her BP reading is not over 140/90.

answer: The correct answer is B. The line is 20 weeks. Hypertension after 20 weeks, with normal BPs before it and no proteinuria or adverse conditions, is gestational hypertension. answer: The correct answer is C. Oral options are labetalol, nifedipine XL or methyldopa. answer: The correct answer is D. Magnesium sulfate is the mainstay of seizure prophylaxis: a 4 g load over 20 minutes, then 1-2 g/h until delivery and for 12-48 h postpartum. It raises the seizure threshold. Eclampsia is pre-eclampsia plus seizures. Nifedipine and hydralazine lower BP but do not prevent seizures.

stem: Which of the following is not a risk factor for vasculogenic Erectile Dysfunction?
answer:
The correct answer is D. ED and coronary heart disease share risk factors — hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hypercholesterolemia, smoking. Blunt pelvic trauma can cause focal stenosis of the common penile or cavernous artery, so it too is vasculogenic.

Alcoholism (and vitamin deficiency) lead to a neurotransmitter deficiency — these are neurogenic, not vasculogenic, causes of ED. The question is testing the mechanism category, not whether alcohol causes ED.

stem: Which of the following is NOT part of crisis care in the immediate aftermath of a sexual assault?

options.html: Use verbal and non-verbal strategies to convey understanding and acceptance.
Provide factual information, normalize symptoms, responses
Anticipate future concerns and discuss coping strategies of other victims
Do not interface with law enforcement

answer:
The correct answer is E. A-D are all part of crisis care. The full list: establish a therapeutic relationship, encourage expression of emotions, provide factual information, anticipate future concerns, adjust immediate role responsibilities, identify and mobilize social supports, explore perceptions of personal safety, and arrange follow-up.

It is also important to interface with medical and law enforcement agencies — as far as the patient desires, or according to legal reporting requirements. Hence E is the incorrect statement.

stem: A 24-year-old primigravid woman presents at 34 weeks after a normal course of pregnancy. She is now presenting with weight gain of 6 lb. in the past 2 weeks. Her BP is 148/100, and her urine contains 2+ protein. The best management of this woman is:

options.html: Ensure fetal well-being, rule out adverse conditions and deliver at term
Induction of labour regardless of gestational age
Monitor fetal well-being and, and administer MgSO4 and antihypertensives

answer:
The correct answer is C. This woman has mild pre-eclampsia (BP >140/90, proteinuria >1+). Management: identify the underlying cause, rule out adverse conditions, ensure fetal wellbeing, increase maternal/fetal surveillance, and deliver at term if investigations are normal.

D and E are the severe pre-eclampsia answers: delivery regardless of gestational age, plus antihypertensives and MgSO4. Compare directly with Q102, where the numbers are severe.

stem: A 30-year-old primigravida at 33 weeks gestation presents with a blood pressure of 160/110 mmHg and 4+ proteinuria. Which of the following is NOT a recommended initial management option for this patient?

options.html: Administration of magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis
Initiation of antihypertensive therapy to lower blood pressure
Delivery of the fetus and placenta as soon as possible
Hospitalization for close monitoring and management

answer:
The correct answer is C. This patient has severe pre-eclampsia — defined as BP ≥ 160/110 mmHg with 4+ proteinuria. Initial management is MgSO4 for seizure prophylaxis, antihypertensives if needed, and hospitalization for close monitoring.

Delivery is the definitive treatment, but not an initial management option — the timing must be weighed against gestational age and disease severity. In general, delivery is recommended after 34 weeks; earlier only if needed to prevent maternal or fetal complications. At 33 weeks, "as soon as possible" is premature.

answer:
The correct answer is B. Risk factors for pre-eclampsia: age <20 or >35, BMI >35, hypertension, renal disease, diabetes, connective tissue disease, previous pre-eclampsia, first pregnancies or pregnancies after an interval of >10 years, and multiple gestations.

Age 33 falls inside the safe window (neither <20 nor >35) — that's the whole point of the option. Note BMI 36 clears the >35 threshold.

stem: Which of the following hormones is not released by the placenta?
answer:
The correct answer is D. The placenta is a major endocrine organ, producing hCG, progesterone, estrogen, hPL, prolactin, inhibin, relaxin and many others.

Oxytocin is the exception: although it crosses and acts on the placenta, it is produced in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary.

Oxytocin released with each let-down reflex

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q80, Q121. Tests [[01 - Antepartum Hemorrhage & Abnormal Placentation]].
stem: Fetal cells present in the maternal circulation on a Kleihauer Betke test suggests
answer:
The correct answer is C. Placental abruption.

The Kleihauer-Betke test detects fetal red cells that have crossed into maternal blood, and for that to happen there must be a breach of the fetomaternal interface — the placenta shearing away from the uterine wall.

That mechanism is what separates abruption from the other causes of antepartum bleeding here. In placenta previa (A) the placenta is implanted over the os and bleeds from the maternal side without necessarily being torn off it. In vasa previa (B) the bleeding is fetal in origin but comes from unprotected fetal vessels crossing the membranes, so it leaves the fetus rather than entering the maternal circulation. Gestational trophoblastic disease (D) and ectopic pregnancy (E) are not placental separation at all.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q108-Q110. Tests [[03 - Approach to Preterm Labor]].
stem: Which of the following is the strongest risk factor for premature labour?
answer:
The correct answer is B. A previous premature delivery is the strongest risk factor for premature labour:

  • 15% risk with 1 previous preterm birth
  • 30% risk with 2 previous preterm births

Other important risk factors: PROM, indications for preterm induction including pre-eclampsia, multiple gestation and placental abnormalities. But 50% of all preterm deliveries have no identifiable cause.

stem: Which of the following does NOT contribute to the initiation of labour?

options.html: High levels of progesterone at term

answer:
The correct answer is D. Progesterone is high throughout pregnancy, but is decreased relative to estrogen at term. It is therefore progesterone withdrawal that initiates labour — not high progesterone levels.

The genuine contributors: oxytocin, prostaglandin, withdrawal of relaxin and prostacyclin, and fetal triggers such as HPA axis activation.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q111-Q115. Tests [[04 - Process of Labor and Birth]].
stem: The second stage of labour is defined as:

options.html: Onset of labour to full dilatation
Cervical dilation of 5 cm with regular uterine contractions
Full dilation to delivery of fetus
Autotransfusion and hemodynamic shift occurring after birth

answer:
The correct answer is C. Second stage = full dilation → delivery of the fetus.

Labour is divided by what the cervix and the fetus are doing, and the second stage is the pushing stage: full dilation through to delivery of the fetus.

The other options are the neighbouring stages, which is what makes them worth knowing rather than eliminating:

  • A is the first stage: onset of labour to full dilation. It subdivides into a latent phase (0–4 cm) and an active phase (4–10 cm).
  • B describes a point inside the active phase, not a stage. True labour is defined by regular uterine contractions causing progressive cervical dilation, so a single dilation figure never defines a stage.
  • D is the third stage, ending with expulsion of the placenta.
  • E is the autotransfusion of the third and fourth stages, when up to 500 mL returns from the uteroplacental unit to the maternal circulation.

Maternal surveillance for complications related to autotransfusion
Assessment of cervical length and administration of progesterone
Insertion of an intrauterine pressure catheter

  • Gentle traction of the umbilical cord
  • Fundal massage, to prevent inversion of the uterus

stem: Which of the following scenarios are NOT an indication for a C-section?
answer:
The correct answer is A. The full list of indications for a C/S: abnormal FHR, fetal malpresentation (e.g. breech), dystocia, maternal HSV/HIV infection, fetal congenital abnormalities, abnormal placentation (e.g. abruption), masses, multiple gestation, cervical cancer.

Maternal diabetes is not itself an indication — though note from Q99 that a diabetic mother with an estimated fetal weight >4.5 kg may need one for macrosomia.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q88, Q99, Q123, Q137. Tests [[05 - Abnormal Labor]].
stem: A 28-year-old nulliparous woman at term presents in active labor with cervical dilation of 8 cm. The fetal heart rate tracing shows a Category II pattern. Which of the following is an appropriate next step in management?

options.html: Continue labor and re-evaluate the fetal heart rate tracing in 30 minutes
Administer a bolus of crystalloid fluid and position the patient in the left lateral decubitus position
Attempt operative vaginal delivery with forceps or vacuum extraction

answer:
The correct answer is B by this year's lecture. Process of Labour and Birth reads a continuous tracing with the SOGC bins - normal / atypical / abnormal - not the American Category I / II / III the stem uses. A Category II tracing is indeterminate, which sits in the SOGC's atypical bin.

⭐ Atypical means act now: institute intrauterine resuscitation, find the cause, and look at the whole clinical picture. The lecture's resuscitation list is fixed: fetal scalp clip, vaginal exam (rule out cord prolapse), left lateral decubitus, oxytocin off, oxygen by mask, and a ~500 mL fluid bolus - which is option B. Delivery is considered only if the pattern persists.

  • A - continuing and re-checking in 30 minutes is the response to a normal tracing, which the lecture says may even be interrupted for up to 30 minutes. It is the workbook's key (see the flag).
  • C and D - expediting delivery is for an abnormal tracing, or an atypical one that persists despite resuscitation.

flags.title: The workbook keys this against this year's lecture
flags.html: The workbook keys A (continue and re-evaluate in 30 minutes) and frames the tracing with the American Category I-III system. This year's Process of Labour and Birth lecture teaches the SOGC normal / atypical / abnormal system, where an indeterminate tracing is atypical and calls for intrauterine resuscitation now. The slides are the reference, so B is the answer used here. Raised by a reader report (issue #25).

Oxytocin is used for prevention of PPH only

answer:
The correct answer is G (B and C). Both distractor statements are true-sounding but have a detail flipped:

  • A has the thresholds swapped. PPH is >1000 mL for C-section or >500 mL for vaginal delivery — or loss of any volume that causes hemodynamic instability.
  • D is wrong because of the word "only". Oxytocin is used for prevention of PPH and as a uterotonic agent to treat an atonic uterus during active hemorrhage.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents to the emergency department 4 days after a vaginal delivery with complaints of heavy vaginal bleeding. She has been passing clots and soaking through 2 pads per hour for the past 12 hours. She denies fever, chills, or abdominal pain. On physical exam, the uterus is tender and enlarged to the level of the umbilicus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is C, retained placenta (retained products of conception). The workbook keys D; see the flag.

⭐ Read the timing first. Bleeding more than 24 hours after delivery is a delayed (secondary) postpartum hemorrhage, and Postpartum Care gives its differential as two things: endometritis or retained products of conception. Its first step is an ultrasound to rule out retained products.

⭐ Then let the stem choose between those two.

  • Retained tissue fits everything here. Placental fragments in the cavity stop the uterus contracting down, so it stays bulky (at the umbilicus on day 4, when it should be well below it) and keeps bleeding heavily, with clots. This is the Tissue of the 4 T's.
  • D, endometritis, is the near-miss. It can cause a tender uterus and a return of bleeding. But it is an infection, and puerperal infection is defined by fever. She denies fever and chills, and the picture is a hemorrhage, not a sepsis.
  • B, uterine atony, is the #1 cause of PPH, but of early PPH, within 24 hours. Four days out, atony is a consequence of retained tissue rather than the diagnosis.
  • A, postpartum hemorrhage, describes what is happening (soaking 2 pads an hour is far more than normal lochia) but is not a cause. The question asks why she is bleeding.

Principle: late postpartum bleeding with a big uterus and no fever is retained tissue until an ultrasound says otherwise. Add a fever and endometritis moves up.

flags.title: The workbook keys this wrong
flags.html: The key prints "125. Answer: D" (endometritis) with no explanation. It then attaches to Q126 an explanation that is plainly about this question and argues for B, uterine atony. From here on, the key's prose runs one question behind its letters (Q144's explanation answers Q126). The workbook is peer-written, and neither of its answers fits the stem. Endometritis needs a fever, which she denies. Atony is an early (<24 h) cause. Postpartum Care works up delayed bleeding by ruling out retained products of conception, which matches a bulky, bleeding uterus with clots. C is the answer used here.

stem: Which of the following options correctly describes placental abruption, placental previa, placental accreta, or vasa previa (choose 1)?

options.html: Vasa previa involves placental invasion into the myometrium, resulting in a need for hysterectomy
Placental abruption can reliably be diagnosed using the Apt test paired with ultrasound.
Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes will result in the leaking of clear fluid and a positive Kleihaur-Betke test.
The treatment for placental accreta is almost always hysterectomy.

answer:
The correct answer is D.

D is correct. A is incorrect -- it describes placental accreta instead of vasa previa (vasa previa = a condition in which fetal blood vessels cross or run near the internal opening of the uterus). B is incorrect -- placental abruption is actually a diagnosis of exclusion. Ultrasound can be used but we learned in module it isn’t always reliable because the collection of blood may have already drained from the uterus. C is incorrect – preterm prelabour rupture of membranes will indeed result in leakage of clear amniotic fluid. However, Kleihaur-Betke test shows when fetal blood entered maternal circulation! PPROM wouldn’t have a positive Kleihaur-Betke test. D is correct – placental accreta will compromise the uterine myometrium so requires hysterectomy. It doesn’t “always” result in hysterectomy because sometimes invasion is local.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q89, Q95, Q98. Tests [[04 - Topics of Antenatal Care]], [[09 - Second Trimester Ultrasound]].
stem: Which of the following fetal assessment tools is the most predictive of perinatal mortality?
answer:
The correct answer is B. FMC, NST and BPP all provide helpful information but really only give a "snapshot" of what is happening with the fetus, and have no effect on perinatal mortality rate.

Umbilical artery Doppler, by contrast, is predictive of morbidity and mortality — and if normal, is associated with a decreased PMR.

weekLabel: Week 6
lectureMeta: Workbook Q80, Q121. Tests [[01 - Antepartum Hemorrhage & Abnormal Placentation]].
stem: Which of the following placental abnormalities may occur from the placenta being implanted too shallowly in the uterus?
answer:
The correct answer is B. Sort the options by what went wrong with implantation:

  • Too deeply → accreta, increta, percreta
  • Wrong location (obstructing the cervical os) → previa
  • Too shallowly → abruption, because a shallowly implanted placenta is more likely to detach from the uterine wall — which can cause hemorrhage, shock, and both fetal and maternal death.

weekLabel: Week 6
lectureMeta: Workbook Q96-Q97. Tests [[02 - Approach to the Small Fetus]].
stem: Which of the following is NOT a common fetal risk in post-term pregnancy?
answer:
The correct answer is A. Post-term pregnancy is defined as pregnancy extending beyond 42 weeks. Risks include macrosomia, birth trauma (shoulder dystocia, prolonged labour, operative delivery), post-maturity syndrome and death.

The direction is the discriminator: post-term pregnancy causes oligohydramnios, not polyhydramnios — which can in turn cause complications such as intolerance of labour.

weekLabel: Week 6
lectureMeta: Workbook Q96-Q97. Tests [[02 - Approach to the Small Fetus]].
stem: An ultrasound is performed to assess fetal growth and reports an asymmetric intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR). The most likely diagnosis is:
answer:
The correct answer is A. Split IUGR by symmetry:

  • Asymmetric — 70-80% of cases; caused by uteroplacental insufficiency (abruption, circumvallate placenta, etc.)
  • Symmetric — 20-30% of cases; most often caused by an early severe insult such as infection or chromosomal abnormality

The logic: a late insult spares the already-grown head (asymmetric); an early insult stunts everything at once (symmetric).

weekLabel: Week 6
lectureMeta: Workbook Q108-Q110. Tests [[03 - Approach to Preterm Labor]].
stem: A 32 year-old primigravida woman presents to the emergency department with premature rupture of membranes at 37 weeks gestation. She does not have a fever and has not yet experienced any contractions. Appropriate management at this time is:

options.html: Tocolysis for 48-72 hours to allow for transfer to birth unit
Observation for spontaneous onset of labour
Immediate induction of labour and administration of MgSO4 and antenatal steroids
Urgent Caesarean section followed by administration of antibiotics
Insertion of an intrauterine pressure monitor

answer:
The correct answer is B. At 37 weeks this is TERM PROM without labour — the gestational age is the whole question. Management of term PROM: allow spontaneous labour, induce with oxytocin at ~6 h if labour does not begin naturally, and GBS prophylaxis.

Contrast the two things the distractors describe:

  • Preterm PROM → antibiotic therapy, antenatal steroids, induction at ~36 weeks
  • Preterm labour → tocolysis × 48 h, antenatal betamethasone, GBS prophylaxis

weekLabel: Week 6
lectureMeta: Workbook Q88, Q99, Q123, Q137. Tests [[05 - Abnormal Labor]].
stem: Management of macrosomia in pregnancy should include all of the following EXCEPT:

options.html: Induction of labour at term with favourable cervix

answer:
The correct answer is C. Umbilical artery Doppler is an important tool for assessing growth restriction — but it is not needed in macrosomia, because placental insufficiency is not the concern here. This is the mirror image of Q98.

Management of macrosomia: rule out causes including gestational diabetes, review nutrition and exercise to manage weight gain, U/S assessment of weight, and possible induction at term if the cervix is favourable. It may also include caesarean section for fetal weight >5 kg, or >4.5 kg in diabetic mothers.

weekLabel: Week 6
lectureMeta: Workbook Q116, Q120, Q125. Tests [[08 - Postpartum Care]].
stem: A 30-year-old woman presents to your office 6 weeks post partum, after giving birth to a healthy baby boy. She has been doing generally well but has noticed that recently she is experiencing pain in her nipples during breastfeeding, and that her nipples appear to be cracked and dry. She has continued with breastfeeding despite this change. Her infant son has been doing well, although she does state that he appears to have patchy white spots on the inside of his mouth. What is the most appropriate management of this patient's problem?

options.html: Topical nystatin to the nipple and infant's mouth
Continue breastfeeding, heat application to breast, fluids, rest

answer:
The correct answer is B. The white patches in the infant's mouth, plus cracked nipples and pain with feeding, make this a candidal infection. Management is topical nystatin cream to the infant's mouth and the areola after each feed for 2 weeks, then qhs for another 2 weeks.

E is the near-miss: oral fluconazole is another option but is not the most appropriate, because it is associated with serious side effects. A treats breast engorgement. C (plus antibiotics) is the treatment for mastitis.

weekLabel: Week 6
lectureMeta: Workbook Q117-Q119. Tests [[09 - Lactation]].
stem: What is the significance of the first 4-6 minutes of each breastfeeding?

options.html: The first 4-6 minutes of each feed contains the highest content of fat, therefore promoting infant satiety and maternal weight loss after pregnancy.
The first 4-6 minutes of each feed has the most impact on hormonal levels, leading to more effective contraception in the post-partum period.
Failure to breastfeed longer than 4-6 minutes at each feed may contribute to breast engorgement and blocked ducts.
The first 4-6 minutes of each feed contains the highest amount of protein.

answer: The correct answer is D. The breast milk in the first 4-6 minutes of each feed contains the majority of the protein for that feed. After this point the milk becomes richer in fat, which promotes satiety — so A has the order exactly backwards.

stem: If present after 7 months, which of the following reflexes suggests cerebral palsy?
answer: The correct answer is B. The ATNR or "fencing" reflex is present in newborns and should be gone by 6 months of age. Its presence after 7 months is ALWAYS abnormal, and typically suggests cerebral palsy.

answer: The correct answer is C. Expectant management is NEVER part of the management of neonatal sepsis. The infant should be started on broad-spectrum antibiotics, which may be narrowed once blood culture results are available.

stem: Which of the following statements regarding normal cardiovascular and pulmonary adaptation is true?

options.html: Surfactant is made in the lungs to increase surface tension within the alveoli
The foramen ovale closes after birth due to increased pulmonary vascular resistance
Lung fluid reabsorption in the neonate is facilitated by ENaC channels within the alveoli
The ductus arteriosus serves to move deoxygenated blood from the right side of the heart to the systemic circulation during fetal development
Normal blood oxygen saturation immediately at birth should be 95+%

answer: The correct answer is C. Surfactant is made in the lungs to decrease surface tension within the alveoli to prevent their collapse. The foramen ovale closes after birth due to decreased pulmonary vascular resistance. The ductus arteriosus serves to move nutrient-rich oxygenated blood from the pulmonary trunk to the aorta during development, allowing the blood to bypass the non-functioning lungs. Normal blood oxygen saturation immediately at birth is 60-65% and normalizes after ~10 minutes.

Preterm infants are at greater risk of respiratory distress syndrome due to immaturity of surfactant production

Broad-spectrum antibiotic use, including antivirals if HSV is suspected
